name: Theerthapureeswarar Temple, Thiruvattathurai (Thirunelvayil Arathurai)
deity: Shiva as Theerthapureeswarar (Arathurainathar), with the Goddess Anandanayaki (Tiripurasundari)
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu on the Vellar, sung by Sambandar in the Tevaram (7th century)
dynasty: Chola country of the Vellar valley, with later additions
summary: On the Vellar near Pennadam, the Arathurai of the Tevaram honours the Lord who sent a pearl palanquin to the weary child-saint Sambandar.

sections.history: Thiruvattathurai is a village in the Tittagudi taluk of Cuddalore district, about six kilometres south-west of Pennadam, and it is the Thirunelvayil Arathurai of the Tevaram. Its Shiva temple is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and stands first, in the traditional order, among the shrines of Nadu Nadu, the middle country between the Chola and Thondai lands. Thirugnana Sambandar sang the Lord here, and the shrine is woven into the story of his journeys as the place where the child-saint was honoured with a pearl palanquin. The river Vellar flows to the south of the temple.
sections.architecture: The temple is a village shrine of the Vellar valley, its sanctum holding Theerthapureeswarar, the lord of the sacred waters, with the Goddess in her own shrine. Its theerthams are the Neela Malar Poigai, the pool of blue flowers, and the Vellar itself. Among its carvings is an old relief that recalls the shrine's great story: a palanquin with an attendant holding up a parasol, the gift that the Lord of Arathurai sent to Sambandar.
sections.legends: The Periya Puranam tradition tells that the young Sambandar, travelling on foot from shrine to shrine after worshipping at Pennadam, grew weary on the road. That night the Lord appeared in dreams to the people of Arathurai and bade them carry to the child a palanquin and parasol adorned with pearls. Sambandar received the gift as the Lord's own grace and came to Arathurai to sing in thanks. Another tradition counts the shrine among seven riverbank temples of the Vellar linked with the Saptarishis.
sections.festivals: The customary Shaiva observances are kept: Maha Shivaratri, the monthly Pradosham worship of Nandi, Arudra Darshanam in Margazhi and the festivals of the Goddess. Devotees of Sambandar remember the gift of the pearl palanquin with special reverence; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Thiruvattathurai is a quiet halt on the Shaiva pilgrim's road through Nadu Nadu, usually visited together with Pennadam nearby. Standing before the old palanquin relief, visitors meet the tenderness of the Tevaram story — a god who noticed a tired child's feet — before walking down to the banks of the Vellar.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruvattathurai lies about 6 km south-west of Pennadam: follow the Virudhachalam–Tittagudi road through Pennadam to Kodikalam, where a branch road leads to the temple. Virudhachalam is the nearest railway junction; Tiruchirappalli and Chennai are the nearest large airports.
